messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame was a 20-year-old African man who had come to the clinic after months of feeling as though something in him had broken and not returned. A single, unmarried doctor, he had prided himself on being calm under pressure, the kind of person patients and coworkers could look to in an emergency. That certainty began to unravel during a combat deployment when his unit came under fire and the air around him changed all at once: gunshots, people shouting, and then the terrifying, unnatural silence that followed when the firing stopped and he could hear his own breathing. He later described that breathing as sharp and labored, as if his chest had forgotten how to work. In the aftermath, those moments returned to him not as a full story but in disconnected pieces that would flash up and then slip away. He found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, and there were stretches he simply could not reconstruct no matter how hard he tried.

Since coming home, Kwame had become convinced that the attack had done more than frighten him. It had destroyed the assumptions he had lived by. He spoke with a quiet bitterness about no longer knowing himself, as if the man who had once wanted to heal people and trust his own judgment had been replaced by someone unfamiliar and permanently altered. What unsettled him most was that ordinary life no longer felt ordinary: sudden silence in a corridor, the pause after a conversation stops, or the sensation of being short of breath during a rushed hospital shift could send him back into the feeling that danger was near. Violence on a television screen or even a heated argument nearby sharpened that sense immediately. Each of these moments seemed to confirm his belief that the world did not work the way he had been taught, and that he had to stay on guard all the time because safety could vanish without warning.

That way of thinking made the memories harder to face. When images or fragments rose up, he would clamp down on them before they became too clear, afraid that if he let the scene come into focus he would be overwhelmed by what it meant about him and about the world. He noticed that the more he tried not to remember, the more the event returned in broken pieces: a flash of dust, the pressure in his chest, the instant of silence after the violence, and then blankness. Those gaps only deepened his sense that something essential was missing, and that he was perhaps missing part of himself with it. In that state, he became even more alert to anything that could hint at threat. He watched faces, listened for changes in tone, and especially reacted to breathlessness in his own body, interpreting it as a sign that danger was close or that he was losing control again.

At work, these moments had begun to intrude into the practical rhythm of being a doctor. During long shifts, when a patient room suddenly went quiet or when he felt himself needing to catch his breath, the old fear returned with enough force that he would excuse himself, step into the hallway, and stand listening for sounds that reassured him. He avoided unnecessary exposure to violence in news reports and shrank away from conversations about conflict, but he could not avoid the hospital environment, where emergencies and silence could appear without warning. Over weeks, that constant watchfulness and the effort to keep the memory at bay left him more exhausted and less certain of his place among colleagues. He said he had started to feel as if he was acting the part of a doctor rather than being one, because the confidence he used to trust no longer felt like his own.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was frightened less by the original event than by the way it kept organizing his present. He was afraid he would keep losing pieces of the memory, and with them whatever was left of his identity, but he was also afraid that if he remembered too much he would be unable to bear what it said about the world. He came in hoping to understand why silence and breathlessness had become so powerful, and whether he could ever feel like himself again without always having to stand guard.

violation_explanations: No paragraph clearly shows triggers/reminders causing negative appraisals; the cues are described as increasing threat and alertness, but not as leading to negative beliefs or appraisals.
No paragraph states that negative appraisals drive the traumatic memory to return or intensify.
No paragraph shows negative appraisals causing triggers or reminders to arise.
No paragraph explicitly shows the traumatic memory leading to negative appraisals; the vignette links memory fragments to fear and threat, but not to beliefs about self or world.
No paragraph explicitly shows the traumatic memory causing triggers/reminders; the cues are presented as eliciting threat, but not as being produced by the memory.
